analysis.one_liner: Requires insurance to cover oral cancer pills as favorably as IV chemotherapy.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate health committee on December 19, 2013 and died there when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many newer cancer drugs come as pills patients take at home, while traditional chemotherapy is given intravenously in a clinic. Insurance plans often cover the clinic treatment generously but charge much more for the pills, leaving patients to pay thousands out of pocket. This bill would require group and individual health plans to cover FDA-approved oral anticancer drugs on terms no less favorable than IV chemotherapy, including similar copays and deductibles, and would block plans from raising out-of-pocket costs to get around it. It also called for a study of how Medicare's drug coverage handles oral cancer medications.
analysis.who_benefits: Cancer patients who take oral chemotherapy pills, and their families. Instead of facing high out-of-pocket costs for pills while paying far less for IV chemo, they would pay the same cost-sharing whichever form of treatment they and their doctor choose.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group and individual health plans covering IV or clinic-administered anticancer drugs to give no less favorable coverage to FDA-approved, patient-administered (oral) anticancer drugs.
Caps cost-sharing for oral cancer drugs at what the plan charges for clinic-administered anticancer drugs, so patients cannot be charged a higher deductible, coinsurance, or copay for pills.
Bars insurers from complying by raising out-of-pocket costs on cancer drugs, reclassifying benefits, or imposing tighter limits on either form of treatment.

Requires plans to notify participants about the required oral drug coverage, and directs the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission to study how closing the Medicare Part D donut hole affects coverage, cost, and access for oral cancer medications.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer health plans, which would have to cover expensive oral cancer drugs on the same terms as clinic-based chemotherapy. Part of the cost could be passed back to all enrollees through premiums.

drawbacks.text: Mandated parity could raise premiums, spreading the cost of expensive oral drugs across all enrollees of a plan.

The bill does not cap the underlying price of oral cancer drugs, so parity means patients pay the same high share of a costly pill as they would for costly infusion drugs rather than lowering drug prices themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For cancer patients, the benefit is concrete: it removes a cost penalty for choosing a pill over an IV bag, which can mean the difference between affording treatment and not. The cost is higher premiums for everyone in affected plans, and the bill leaves drug prices themselves untouched. It is a narrow insurance-design fix, not a drug-price fix.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the final weeks of 2013 and referred to the Senate health committee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Al Franken introduced the bill on December 19, 2013, with Sen. Mark Kirk as cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The committee took no further action, and no roll-call vote on the bill occurred before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans are better off because the bill died: they never had to put oral cancer pills on the same cost-sharing terms as IV chemotherapy. Cancer patients who pay high out-of-pocket costs for oral drugs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, who never had to cover pills equally

for.name: Sen. Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cancer Treatment Parity Act of 2013 on December 19, 2013.

for.name: Sen. Mark Kirk
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan two-senate effort.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 19, 2013 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The two-senator sponsorship was bipartisan — one Democrat and one Republican — and no one actively opposed it; the bill simply died from inaction.

industries.note: Insurers would have had to cover oral cancer drugs with cost-sharing no worse than IV chemotherapy, a mandate many plans avoided so patients on pills bore higher costs. The bill died, so plans kept that discretion.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical makers of oral cancer drugs
industries.note: Parity requirements make oral cancer drugs more accessible and affordable to patients, expanding the market for these products, though the bill does not raise or lower their prices.
ERISA plans would face the same coverage mandate, potentially raising benefit costs for employers, but the bill never advanced.
